title: He Has Not Come to Punish Him
deck: O'Brien does not want Winston merely to obey. He wants Winston to experience the Party's judgment as his own.
body: Edition note: Complete English translation of the Chinese essay. Full-book spoilers.
Winston is beaten for a long time in the Ministry of Love.
At first it is ordinary beating. Several men take turns until he confesses. He does confess: to everything, to things he has not done, implicating people he does not know. He will sign anything.
And it does not end.
Later, O'Brien arrives.
Beside him is a dial that controls the intensity of Winston's pain. He sits beside the bed and talks to Winston, with great patience.
The sense of his opening words is: do you know how long you have been here? Do you know why I am spending so much time on you?
He has not come to punish him
To understand this passage, we must first be clear about one thing: there is no hatred in O'Brien's attitude toward Winston.
He is not angry. He does not find Winston detestable. He speaks to him like a doctor, or a teacher. Sometimes even like a friend.

He gives him water between bouts of torture. He corrects his mistakes as though correcting a pupil's arithmetic. He knows what Winston is thinking, even more clearly than Winston knows it himself. He says he has been studying Winston for seven years.
Seven years.
A senior Inner Party official spends seven years studying a minor Outer Party clerk.
This is on a different scale from an interrogation. It is an engineering project.
And O'Brien states what the project consists of: they do not intend to punish him. They intend to cure him.
He says: we are not satisfied with passive obedience, or even with the most abject submission.
He says: before we destroy you, we will first make you one of us.
He says: we will not allow a single mistaken thought to exist anywhere in the world, however deeply hidden and however harmless.
Why obedience is not enough
Now we come to the essay's first central point, the thing that sets this book apart from every other story of tyranny.
An ordinary tyranny wants obedience.

It does not care what you think inside, as long as you comply. You may hate it, curse it in private, know inwardly that it is lying. As long as you turn up for work, pay your taxes on time, and stay off the streets.
Such rule has one characteristic: it assumes that you and it are two separate things. Wanting to suppress you means acknowledging that there is something there to be suppressed.
And that acknowledgment is itself a gap.
Someone forced to obey always keeps a sentence inside: “I am being forced.” That sentence belongs to him. It has not been taken away. Every day he obeys, he knows that he is obeying.
O'Brien intends to take away precisely that sentence.

He tells Winston very clearly: the old tyrannies failed because all they achieved was making people afraid to speak. People confessed outwardly while refusing inwardly. Then they died, and at the moment of death they were free.
We do not make that mistake, he says.
What they want is this: you are not forced to say that two plus two equals five. You actually see five.
The things he says
O'Brien speaks at length about the Party's purpose. It is one of the most famous passages in the book, and one of the easiest to read too quickly.
What does Winston think the Party is doing it for? He tries an answer: for the people's good, to make everyone happy, because you believe this is a better way.
O'Brien calls him a fool.
Then he gives the answer: the Party pursues power entirely for power's own sake.
Not for money, not for pleasure, not for long life, not to make the world better. Power is not the means. Power is the end.
He says something more precise still: the purpose of persecution is persecution. The purpose of torture is torture. The purpose of power is power.
Then comes the most famous image. Winston asks him what the future will look like.
O'Brien says: if you want a picture of the future, imagine a boot stamping on a human face, and going on stamping forever.
Why this speech is so difficult to face
This passage is often read as a villain's deranged manifesto, a passage the author uses to expose the nature of totalitarianism.
It is much harder to face than that.
There are two difficulties.
First, O'Brien is not mad.

He is intelligent, calm, cultivated. He has read all the books he ought to have read. He is even one of the authors of the forbidden book. He knows exactly how the system works, which lies it tells, whether each of the Party's theories holds up.
He knows the whole truth, and then chooses this side.

That blocks a familiar escape route. We often comfort ourselves by saying that people who do evil have been misled, that they are ignorant, that they are deceiving themselves. O'Brien has been misled about nothing.
Second, what he wants has no limit.

A ruler with a particular objective can be negotiated with. If he wants money, it can be given. If he wants status, it can be arranged. If he wants a country to become powerful, then once it is powerful, there will come a day when he stops.
But “power itself” is an aim that can never be satisfied.
Because what would count as enough? There is no standard. So the machinery can only keep pressing forward, into the deepest place: into a person's mind.
O'Brien says something that brings this logic to its conclusion. How, he asks, can one person be certain that he has power over another?
Make him suffer, he says.
Because if the other person acts willingly, you cannot know whether it is your power or his own desire at work. Only by making him do what he does not want to do does power become visible.
So the machinery must keep inflicting pain, not because it is cruel, but because this is the only way it can confirm its own existence.
Two plus two
The first essay discussed the sentence Winston writes in his diary: freedom means being free to say that two plus two equals four.
O'Brien comes to deal specifically with that sentence.
He holds up four fingers and asks Winston how many he sees.
Winston says four. O'Brien turns the dial, and the pain suddenly intensifies.
The question again. Four again. More pain.
O'Brien says: I want you to see five.
Winston says he cannot lie and say that he sees five.
But a lie is not what O'Brien wants.
He makes this very clear: saying five is not enough. You must actually see five.
This goes on for a long time. The book describes a moment when Winston really is no longer certain. He looks at the hand and does not know how many fingers he sees.
O'Brien says this is progress.
What is happening here?
Now we come to the essay's most important layer.
The first essay described the system as closing gaps: gaps in language, in feeling, in fact.
Here it is closing the last one.
Two plus two equals four is the last thing Winston has. What makes it special is that it requires no one's permission.

You can take a person's freedom, property, friends, lover, memories, name. But the answer to two plus two remains what it is in his mind. It depends on no record, no recognition, no outside condition.
This is the last place within a person that needs no one else's permission.
It is precisely this place that O'Brien wants.
And the means he uses is not logic. He does not debate Winston. He does not try to prove that two plus two equals five.
He uses pain, and time.
He asks again and again, inflicts pain again and again, until the person's certainty begins to loosen. He is not persuaded. He is worn down.
This passage shows something deeply uncomfortable: a person's certainty about the world can be dismantled by physical means.
Not because the certainty is mistaken. Two plus two really does equal four. But because certainty itself depends on a person's condition to sustain it, and that condition can be destroyed.
And even this is not enough.
The final step takes place in Room 101.
O'Brien says that Room 101 contains the worst thing in the world. And for each person, that thing is different.
It is whatever that person fears most.
What Winston fears most is rats.
They fasten a cage against his face. There are rats inside, with a door between them and him. O'Brien's hand rests on the latch.
Winston cries out.
What he cries is: let them bite Julia! Not me! Her!
The book is very precise about this: at that moment, he genuinely wants those creatures to attack the other person. He is willing to exchange her for himself.
This is what they want.
Not his confession: he confessed long ago. Not his betrayal of the organization: the organization may not even exist.
What they want is for him, at that moment, willingly and from within, to thrust another person forward.
Because once he has cried those words, he can never take them back. He can no longer tell himself, “In my heart I still love her,” because he has heard himself say them.
In the second essay, Julia said: they can make you say anything, but they cannot get inside you.
It is one of the most moving statements in the book, and it is wrong.
Room 101 exists specifically to prove it wrong.
They meet once more afterward
After his release, Winston encounters Julia in a park.
They stand there and exchange a few words.
She says she betrayed him too. She says she cried out in the same way, said the same thing: transfer the pain to the other person.
She says: you discover that you really mean it.
Then she says something harsher still: afterward, you no longer feel the same about that person.
They have little to say to one another. They part politely.
The passage is very short, over in a few pages, and it is the coldest place in the whole book.
Because the Party does not merely want to lock them both up. It wants them to have nothing to say when they meet.
Next
After his release, Winston sits in the Chestnut Tree Café. He drinks a great deal of gin. No one bothers him, and no one talks to him.
He still has a sinecure at the Ministry of Truth. His salary continues to be paid.
On the last page, the telescreen announces a great victory at the front. He raises his head, and tears run down his face.
The main narrative ends: He had won the victory over himself. He loved Big Brother.
This is the most complete defeat in the history of literature.
The first essay asked a question: this is an attempt at closure, but can it succeed?
The main narrative answers: it has succeeded.
But the book contains something else, after the main narrative ends.
The next essay will discuss that.
George Orwell, Nineteen Eighty-Four, published in 1949. Names and terms in the Chinese essay follow Dong Leshan's translation.

review.full_reread: Read all four Chinese bodies and all four complete en translations, titles, decks and index. Reread every changed unit against the final approved wording and its surrounding argument. Earlier review evidence is retained in review_history, not current pending status.
review.structure: All paragraph, heading and inline-emphasis boundaries preserved; all unamended prose units unchanged.
review.interpretive_boundaries: Original authorial judgments retained. Source observations outside the approved change set remain historical context; this pass makes no new claim of exhaustive independent novel or publication-history verification.
semantic_checks: Photograph: conscious recognition and concealment, then destruction after about ten minutes through fear; no reflex or pre-awareness claim remains.
Private life: the Brotherhood attempt remains explicit, while value exceeds usefulness to resistance; deliberate suppression of sexual pleasure is not confused with a forgotten prohibition.
Dress is a future intention while Julia remains in overalls; lipstick replaces the invented worn dress in both sensory examples.
Julia rejects the earlier dead claim and repeats it only just before arrest; present life is distinguished from distant political victory.
Cross-references now point to essay three; forbidden book arrives later through a briefcase exchange.
Pain is controlled by a dial, without asserting an electrical mechanism; the two final sentences are the ending of the main narrative.
Publication: American Book-of-the-Month Club deletion request and refusal; the importance of final placement is explicitly the essay’s reading.

Proles: less intensive ideological training coexists with surveillance and removal of threats; no blanket illiteracy claim; the courtyard is reached by power without exhausting the meaning of the song.

Preserved the complete room/trap/real-experience argument, authorial claim that past events cannot be undone, stronger judgment about totality, and cautious appendix reading without supplying a new proof or ending.

review_history.stage: Complete-translation review before approved source corrections

review.coverage: All 116 units translated in order, including nine headings, the seven-year scale, the entire power-for-power argument, arithmetic, Room 101, the park reunion, and the next-essay transition.
prior_edition_findings: The previous approximately 503-word version omitted the interrogation's full progression, the two difficulties in O'Brien's position, the dependency of certainty on bodily condition, and the detailed aftermath between the lovers.

Its new section on genuine teaching versus counterfeit teaching and a regime's dependence on producing interior places to invade changed the author's argument. Neither has been imported into the complete translation.

source_questions.issue: The Chinese specifies electric shocks. The novel describes an instrument and dial controlling pain, but the passages inspected do not explicitly identify the mechanism as electrical. Translated faithfully; no unsupported technical details added beyond the source.

The novel brings the cage-mask against Winston's cheek and closes rather than opens its door after his cry. The Chinese compresses this into fastening the cage to his face. Retained without adding an actual rat attack.

Willingly describes the inward wish produced under torture, not free consent or absence of coercion. The surrounding description of terror is kept so that the translation does not exculpate the torturer.
The novel explicitly gives him a better-paid sinecure after release; the Chinese names the Ministry of Truth and says his salary continues. Retained pending any author clarification.

review.style: The author's certainty argument, short emphatic lines, and cold reunion are restored without adding a separate theory of education or a claim that Winston's execution occurs on the final page.
review.full_reread: All source and translated units were reread together as the four-essay batch; structure, emphasis, voice, transitions, and unresolved source claims were checked.
